opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, research and product aren't two separate worlds. The best research usually starts from a real problem, something people actually struggle with, and the product is just the most honest test of whether you solved it.

Early in my career I cared mostly about the paper: does the method work, does it beat the baseline, is the idea elegant. Over time I realized a demo that works on a curated benchmark is very different from something people use every day. When we built image synthesis tools where you could sketch a rough layout and get a photorealistic landscape, the research result was exciting. But once artists and ordinary users started playing with it, we learned much more: what they found intuitive, where the model broke, what controls they wanted. That feedback loop changed which research questions I thought were important.

So my approach has a few parts. First, pick problems where there's a clear path to impact, even if it's long. I'm drawn to foundational capabilities like generative models and, more recently, world models for physical AI, because they unlock many downstream products rather than just one.

Second, build things other people can build on. Often the most effective "product" from a research team is a platform, an open model, or a toolkit. If we release a world foundation model, roboticists, autonomous driving teams, and developers can fine-tune it for their own needs. That multiplies the impact far beyond what our small team could do alone.

Third, stay close to users and to engineering early. A lot of research dies in the handoff, where a researcher throws a prototype over the wall and expects a product team to make it robust. It works much better when researchers care about data pipelines, inference speed, and failure cases from the start. Those "boring" constraints often lead to genuinely new research ideas.

And finally, be patient but honest. Some ideas aren't ready yet. The compute isn't there, the data isn't there, or the model isn't reliable enough. Part of the job is knowing when to keep pushing on the science and when something is mature enough to put in people's hands. When you get that timing right, research and product reinforce each other, and that's the most fun part of this work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about going from research to product, I think the first thing to say is that these are really two different mindsets, and you have to be honest about which one you're in at any given moment.

In research, your job is to find something new. You're rewarded for showing that an idea works, even if it only works on a benchmark or in a demo. The bar is "this is possible." In product, the bar is completely different. The bar is "this works every time, for a user who doesn't care how it works, at a cost that makes sense." A model that produces a beautiful result nine times out of ten is a great paper and a terrible product, because the user remembers the tenth time.

So the way I approach it is, I try to start from the problem the user actually has, not from the technique I happen to be excited about. For a long time at NVIDIA, a lot of my work was in generative models for images and video, and the temptation is always to say, we have this new model, what can we do with it? But the better question is, who is going to use this tomorrow morning, and what is the thing they are struggling with today? For example, with simulation and digital twins, people building robots or autonomous systems don't have enough real data, and collecting it is expensive or dangerous. That's a real, painful problem. Generative models happen to be a good answer to it. When the problem and the technology line up like that, the product almost designs itself.

The second thing is that you have to think about the whole system, not just the model. The model is maybe twenty percent of the product. The rest is data pipelines, evaluation, latency, safety, how it fits into the tools people already use. A researcher often underestimates this part. I've learned to respect it. The teams that are good at this, the engineers and product people, they are solving problems that are just as hard as the research problems, they're just less glamorous.

And the third thing, which I think is particular to this moment in AI, is that the technology is moving so fast that you can't plan a product for three years out assuming the model stays the same. You have to build in a way where you can swap in the next generation of models without rebuilding everything. That changes how you think about architecture, about APIs, about what you promise customers.

Finally, I'd say the best thing about doing both is that product pulls research in the right direction. When you ship something and real users break it, you learn which research problems actually matter. A lot of my best research questions came from watching something fail in practice. So I don't see it as research first, then product. It's more of a loop, and the faster that loop turns, the better both sides get.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what problem you’re solving for someone. In research, you might focus on whether a method is new or whether it improves a benchmark. For a product, you have to ask: Is that improvement useful? Can someone get a good result reliably, and is it worth the time and cost?

With AI, a compelling demo can be a starting point, but there’s a lot of work between that demo and something people can depend on. You need to understand where the model fails and how the user can correct it. Sometimes giving people better control is more valuable than improving the model’s average performance.

So I see research and product development as a feedback loop. Research opens up possibilities, and putting those possibilities in front of users helps you discover which problems you actually need to solve next.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with asking what problem we’re solving for the user. In research, you might focus on a new capability or a better benchmark result. For a product, that capability has to fit into something people actually want to do, and it has to work reliably enough that they keep using it.

I think the process needs a tight feedback loop. You build a prototype, put it in people’s hands, and learn where your assumptions were wrong. Sometimes the model needs to improve. Sometimes the interface is the problem, or the latency, or the cost. Those constraints can also lead to interesting research questions.

So I see research and product development as connected. Research opens up possibilities, and working with users helps you decide which possibilities are worth pursuing.
